title: Beyond Data Silos: Powering the Autonomous Enterprise with SAP's Next-Generation Data Fabric and AI
author: RanjeetKr
text:
The next era of enterprise transformation is not just about making data available. It is about making data intelligent, contextual, trusted, and actionable. 
 Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming how businesses operate. From demand forecasting and supply chain optimization to financial planning and customer engagement, AI agents are moving beyond generating insights to actively supporting business decisions and executing complex workflows. 
 But there is one fundamental challenge: AI is only as intelligent as the business context it understands. 
 Enterprise data is often scattered across applications, databases, data warehouses, and cloud platforms. Even when organizations have access to vast amounts of information, disconnected systems, inconsistent master data, and fragmented business definitions make it difficult for AI to understand how the business actually operates. 
 At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced a new wave of innovations in SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) to address this challenge and accelerate the journey toward the autonomous enterprise. 
 With advancements in open lakehouse architecture, zero-copy data sharing, enterprise master data management, and business knowledge modeling, SAP is taking an important step toward creating an intelligent data foundation where AI agents can understand business operations, make informed decisions, and act with greater autonomy and confidence. 
 Let's explore the innovations shaping this transformation. 
 1. Breaking Data Silos: An Open Lakehouse Built for the AI Era 

 Enterprise data should not be restricted by platforms, storage locations, or technology boundaries. However, traditional data architectures often require organizations to replicate information across multiple systems, creating additional costs, operational complexity, and inconsistent data. 
 SAP is addressing this challenge by strengthening its open lakehouse foundation through the completed acquisition of Dremio. 
 The vision is simple: make enterprise data accessible wherever it resides, without constantly moving or duplicating it. 
 Key innovations include: 

 Open lakehouse architecture: Native Apache Iceberg support and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris provide an open foundation for discovering, governing, and sharing enterprise data. 

 Zero-copy data sharing: SAP BDC Connect enables interoperability with platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, Google Cloud, AWS, and Microsoft, minimizing unnecessary data duplication. 

 Federated data access: Powered by Dremio's high-performance SQL query engine, organizations can query distributed data across SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without physically moving it. 

 Autonomous query optimization: Dremio Reflections intelligently optimize query performance by learning workload patterns and automatically precomputing frequently accessed results. 
 An especially exciting development is the integration with Joule Work, allowing business users to ask complex questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in trusted enterprise data. 
 The business impact: Less time managing data pipelines, fewer data silos, faster analytics, and a scalable data foundation for AI agents operating across enterprise environments. 
 2. SAP and Databricks: Accelerating the Next Generation of Data and AI Innovation 
 The future of enterprise AI requires collaboration between business applications, data engineering platforms, and advanced AI technologies. 
 SAP's expanded partnership with Databricks brings additional industry-leading capabilities into SAP Databricks within SAP Business Data Cloud. 
 The expanded capabilities include: 

 Lakeflow 

 Agent Bricks 

 Unity Gateway 

 Lakebase 
 Through SAP Application Data Foundation, organizations can access SAP application data directly within their preferred SAP BDC engine, including SAP Databricks. 
 This creates an opportunity to combine the rich business semantics of SAP data with the advanced analytics and AI capabilities of Databricks. 
 Consider a real-world manufacturing scenario. 
 A manufacturer wants to predict future product demand, optimize inventory, and improve supply chain efficiency. 
 Traditionally, this could involve extracting historical sales data, integrating inventory information, combining external market intelligence, and building complex data pipelines before developing forecasting models. 
 With SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Databricks, data professionals can access SAP data, enrich it with third-party information, and create custom data products on a semantically rich foundation. 
 AI models can then generate forecasts that are aligned with the business logic and relationships already embedded in SAP systems. 
 The business impact: Accelerated AI development, reduced integration complexity, lower total cost of ownership, and faster realization of business value from cloud transformation. 
 3. SAP Reltio: Turning Fragmented Master Data into a Trusted 360-Degree Business View 
 One of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption is inconsistent master data. 
 Imagine an organization where the same customer exists in multiple systems with different customer IDs, addresses, names, and transaction histories. 
 A human employee might recognize that these records represent the same customer. But an AI agent needs reliable entity resolution and connected business relationships to reach the same conclusion. 
 This is where SAP Reltio becomes important. 
 Following the completion of its acquisition, SAP Reltio is now generally available within SAP Business Data Cloud, bringing multi-domain Master Data Management (MDM) capabilities natively into the business data fabric. 
 Its AI-based entity resolution capabilities help organizations: 

 Identify and reconcile duplicate records across SAP and non-SAP systems. 

 Harmonize inconsistent customer, supplier, and product information. 

 Build unified 360-degree views of critical business entities. 

 Connect business attributes, relationships, and interactions. 

 Publish trusted entity profiles as governed data products. 
 The significance goes beyond traditional master data management. 
 When Joule and Joule Agents access unified business entity profiles, they gain a more complete understanding of customers, suppliers, products, and their relationships across the enterprise. 
 For example, a customer service agent can potentially understand a customer's purchase history, outstanding invoices, service interactions, and business relationships through connected and trusted information. 
 The business impact: Better data quality, improved decision-making, stronger customer intelligence, and a reliable foundation for context-aware enterprise AI. 
 4. SAP Knowledge Graph and Ontology Manager: Giving AI Agents the Context to Think and Act 
 This is arguably one of the most important developments in SAP's journey toward the autonomous enterprise. 
 AI agents do not simply need access to information. They need to understand what that information represents, how different business entities are connected, and which business rules govern their decisions. 
 For example, knowing that an invoice is overdue is useful. But understanding the customer associated with that invoice, the agreed payment terms, the credit exposure, and the organization's collections policies is what enables meaningful business action. 
 SAP Knowledge Graph provides this connected business understanding by linking enterprise entities, relationships, and business rules. 
 At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced SAP Business Data Cloud Ontology Manager , an AI-assisted experience that enables organizations to create domain-specific views of SAP Knowledge Graph. 
 Rather than exposing an entire enterprise knowledge model to every AI agent, organizations can create curated views containing only the information relevant to a particular business scenario. 
 Consider a collections AI agent. 
 To support collections operations effectively, the agent needs to understand: 

 Customer relationships. 

 Outstanding invoices. 

 Payment terms. 

 Credit risk. 

 Financial transactions. 

 Relevant business rules and policies. 
 Using Ontology Manager, organizations can create a dedicated collections domain view that connects these entities and relationships. 
 Joule Agents can then use this context to generate more relevant answers, recommendations, and business actions. 
 Even more importantly, these domain-specific views inherit business definitions and governance from SAP Knowledge Graph. 
 This means organizations can reuse the same business semantics across collections, cash flow management, order management, and other business scenarios without repeatedly redefining the underlying concepts. 
 The business impact: More intelligent AI agents, consistent business semantics, reusable enterprise knowledge, and decisions grounded in how the organization actually operates. 
 5. The Bigger Picture: SAP Is Moving Beyond Data Management Toward Business Intelligence for Autonomous Operations 
 The real significance of these announcements is not any individual technology or product integration. It is how these capabilities come together to create a unified foundation for enterprise intelligence. 
 Consider how the different innovations complement each other: SAP innovation Role in the autonomous enterprise 

 Dremio Open Lakehouse 
 Makes distributed enterprise data accessible 

 Apache Iceberg and Polaris 
 Enables open data management and discovery 

 SAP BDC Connect 
 Supports zero-copy data sharing 

 SAP Databricks 
 Accelerates advanced analytics and AI development 

 SAP Reltio 
 Establishes trusted, unified business entities 

 SAP Knowledge Graph 
 Connects enterprise data with business meaning 

 Ontology Manager 
 Creates reusable, domain-specific business context 

 Joule and Joule Agents 
 Turn business context into intelligent assistance and action 
 Together, these capabilities establish a powerful foundation for the next generation of enterprise AI. 
 The transformation can be understood through four interconnected layers: 
 The foundation of an autonomous enterprise 
 AI & Autonomous Actions 
 Joule · Joule Agents · Intelligent business workflows 
 Business Context & Semantics 
 SAP Knowledge Graph · Ontology Manager · SAP Reltio 
 Data Integration & Interoperability 
 SAP BDC Connect · Zero-copy sharing · SAP Databricks 
 Open Data Foundation 
 Dremio · Apache Iceberg · Apache Polaris · Distributed data sources 
 Conceptual representation of how the announced capabilities work together, not an official SAP reference architecture. 
 This approach shifts the enterprise data strategy from simply collecting and processing information to creating a connected business intelligence ecosystem. 
 6. What Enterprises Should Take Away from These Announcements 
 For business leaders, enterprise architects, data engineers, and AI transformation teams, these innovations highlight several important priorities: 
 1. Think beyond traditional data integration. Build open architectures that allow data to remain accessible across platforms without unnecessary duplication. 
 2. Treat business context as a strategic asset. High-quality data alone is not enough. Business definitions, relationships, policies, and semantics must also be available to AI. 
 3. Invest in trusted master data. AI-driven decisions require consistent customer, supplier, product, and financial information across systems. 
 4. Make enterprise knowledge reusable. Domain-specific ontologies can help organizations develop AI agents that understand individual business processes without rebuilding business semantics for every use case. 
 5. Move from AI experimentation to business execution. The ultimate objective is to enable AI agents to support real business workflows with the appropriate governance, context, and controls. 
 Conclusion: The Future Belo

title: Preview report options are not working in Plateau Report Designer tool
author: PTecnico
text:
Dear Experts 
 After importing the custom report into the Plateau Report Designer tool (PRD), the user is unable to preview the report and encounters an error message: 
 " HTTP ERROR: 500. Problem accessing /viewer/frameset. Reason: Server Error. Powered by Jetty ." 
 Reproducing the Issue 
 Access the Plateau Report Design tool > 
 Import custom report > 
 Select 'Run' > View Report > Choose the available options > 
 Observe an error in the browser stating: " HTTP ERROR: 500. Problem accessing /viewer/frameset. Reason: Server Error. Powered by Jetty ". 

 The configuration for PlateauReportDesigner.ini file is: 
 -startup 
 plugins/org.eclipse.equinox.launcher_1.3.0.v20140415-2008.jar 
 --launcher.library 
 plugins/org.eclipse.equinox.launcher.win32.win32.x86_1.1.200.v20140603-1326 
 -vm 
 C:\Program Files (x86)\Java\jre1.8.0_501\bin\javaw.exe 
 -data 
 E:\Plateau Report Designer\Workspace 
 -vmargs 
 -Xms40m 
 -Xmx256m 
 -XX:MaxPermSize=128m 
 What is the possible cause of this error: 
 In the note 3657398. only say: 
 https://me.sap.com/notes/3657398 
 Cause 
 The issue is related to Java and occurs specifically with custom reports' preview in the browser from the PRD tool. 
 Resolution 
 This issue falls outside the scope of our support, as it pertains to a custom reports' preview in the browser from the PRD tool, rather than the Learning Management System application. 
 To address this scenario, we recommend the following options: 
 You can still build the report in PRD and import it into Learning Administration, even if the preview functionality does not work for reports. 
 You may consider reaching out to your IT team to explore potential solutions. Alternatively, if you require further assistance from SAP, you can contact the Professional Services team for further assistance.

title: HCM Job Architecture Harmonization in M&A Projects
author: manubhutani
text:
HCM Job Architecture Harmonization in M&A Projects 
 1. Purpose and when to harmonize 
 An acquired workforce arrives with its own jobs, levels, titles, and pay structures. A lift-and-shift carries those over as they are by creating placeholders. Harmonization maps them into the acquirer’s job architecture so both populations run on a single, consistent structure in the target system. This guide covers how harmonization is carried out, the practices that work, how clients typically approach it, and the issues they run into. 

 Dimension 
 Lift-and-shift 
 Harmonize 

 What happens to acquired jobs 
 Loaded as separate job codes, levels, and grades 
 Mapped to the acquirer’s (or a combined) job codes, levels, and grades 

 Speed to Day 1 
 Faster; few decisions needed 
 Slower; needs design, compensation, and legal decisions and approvals 

 Effort later 
 Higher: two structures to maintain, split reporting 
 Lower: one structure, one governance process 

 Employee impact 
 Little visible change 
 Possible title, level, or grade changes; needs careful communication 

 Best fit 
 Short transition period, or the acquired entity stays separate 
 Workforce will be integrated long-term with shared reporting, pay cycles, and mobility 

 How to decide whether harmonization is the right call? 
 The acquired employees will sit in the same organization, reporting lines, and manager population as existing employees. 
 Compensation planning, promotion cycles, and performance processes will be shared. 
 Leadership expects combined workforce reporting by job family, level, or grade. 
 The acquirer wants one career framework and wants to avoid maintaining two architectures. 
 Timeline of HCM TSA Exit 

 2. Anatomy of a job architecture 
 A job architecture is the structure that organizes every role in the company. Harmonization means aligning each of these components, not just job codes. 

 Component 
 What it defines 
 SF EC representation 

 Job family and function 
 Broad groupings of work (Finance, Engineering, HR, Operations) 
 Job Function; job family via Job Profile Builder or a custom object 

 Job profile / job code 
 The standard definition of a role 
 Job Classification (job code) foundation object 

 Level 
 Scope and seniority within a family 
 Job Level (picklist or foundation object) 

 Grade and pay structure 
 Pay ranges, bands, or steps tied to level 
 Pay Grade, Pay Range, Pay Components 

 Titles 
 Job title (system) vs. business title (what people see) 
 Job title on job information; business title as a separate field 

 Classification attributes 
 Exempt/non-exempt, EEO category, regulatory or country-specific classification 
 Attributes on Job Classification; country-specific fields 

 Career paths 
 How people move across levels and families 
 Job Profile Builder or career content, or documented outside the system 

 Position structure (if used) 
 Seats in the org tied to a job code 
 Position Management objects 
 3. High Level Source to target mapping 

 Common source concept 
 Typical SF EC target 

 Job Family Group 
 Job Function or grouping in Job Profile Builder 

 Job Family 
 Job family / sub-function (Job Profile Builder or custom object) 

 Job Profile 
 Job Classification (job code) 

 Management Level 
 Job Level 

 Compensation Grade / Grade Profile 
 Pay Grade and Pay Range 

 Worker type / time type 
 Employee Class, Employment Type, Regular/Temporary 

 Position or job management staffing model 
 Position Management on or off 

 Worker-level business title 
 Business title field 

 Profile attributes (exempt status, EEO) 
 Job Classification attributes 

 4. Key design decisions 
 These decisions shape the step-by-step approach that follows. Agree them early, ideally before detailed mapping begins. 

 Decision 
 Options 
 Guidance 

 Level alignment 
 Adopt the acquirer’s levels, or map by scope 
 Match on scope of impact and accountability; calibrate on a sample of roles with business leaders 

 Titles 
 Keep legacy titles for a period, or convert at go-live 
 Separate the system job title from the business title to reduce friction for employees 

 Pay mapping 
 Map by grade equivalence, or by pay range overlap 
 Use range overlap; set a policy for out-of-range incumbents (hold, freeze, review at next cycle) 

 Exempt / non-exempt status 
 Keep source classification, or reassess 
 Treat any reclassification as a legal decision with overtime and payroll implications 

 Country rules 
 Single global mapping, or country exceptions 
 Plan exceptions where local law, collective agreements, or works council rights apply (for example Germany, France, and the Netherlands) 

 Number of job codes 
 Consolidate aggressively, or preserve granularity 
 Consolidate duplicates, but avoid losing granularity needed for market pricing and compliance 

 Staffing model 
 Position management or job management 
 Decide early; it affects headcount control, approvals, and reporting 

 Effective date 
 At go-live, or after the transition period or next pay cycle 
 Choose based on legal review, pay cycle timing, and what employees can absorb 

 History 
 Keep legacy codes in history, or remap 
 Keep a legacy-to-target reference so reporting can bridge both 

 5. How harmonization is done: step by step 
 Common issues clients face, and how to handle them, are noted under each step. 
 Step 1: Discover and inventory 
 Extract all jobs from the source: job code, title, family, level, grade, exempt status, country, and headcount by job. 
 Collect the acquirer’s architecture: job catalog, leveling guide, pay structures, title conventions, and any market pricing data. 
 Identify countries with local requirements, such as works council involvement or collective agreements. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Messy job inventory. Duplicate, inactive, and single-person job codes build up over years. Clean and consolidate them here, and agree rules for legacy and single-incumbent codes before mapping. 
 Step 2: Set design principles and the target model 
 Choose the target: the acquirer’s architecture, a hybrid with extensions for specialist roles, or a new combined model. 
 Agree with the principles, for example: no pay reductions, no automatic title demotions, minimize new job codes, country compliance first. 
 Decide title policy, the level-matching method, and who owns the architecture after go-live. 
 Get executive approval of the principles before detailed mapping begins. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Unclear ownership. There is often no single owner of job architecture on the acquirer side. Name an owner and an approver at kickoff, and start a decision log. 
 Staffing model mismatch. Source and target may handle positions and headcount differently. Decide the model early, and confirm during testing that approvals and headcount reporting behave as intended. 
 Timeline pressure. Harmonization decisions often take longer than the build and test windows. Prioritize high-headcount jobs, and use an interim crosswalk with phased employee-facing changes if needed. 
 Step 3: Build the crosswalk 
 The crosswalk is the core deliverable: a line by line mapping from every source job to a target job. Match on scope, accountability, required skills, and typical pay range , not on titles alone. 

 Crosswalk field 
 Purpose 

 Source job code, title, family, level, grade 
 Identify the starting point 

 Headcount and countries 
 Prioritizes review and shows where local rules apply 

 Target job code, title, family, level, grade 
 The proposed destination 

 Match type 
 One to one, many to one, one to many, no match, or exception 

 Confidence (high / medium / low) 
 Focus review time on uncertain matches 

 Pay impact 
 Flags incumbents outside the target range 

 Legal or works council flag 
 Marks items needing consultation or counsel review 

 Approver and status 
 Creates accountability and an audit trail 

 Match type 
 Description 
 Typical treatment 

 One-to-one 
 Source job equals a target job 
 Map directly 

 Many-to-one 
 Several source jobs collapse into one target job 
 Consolidate - check that pay and scope differences are acceptable 

 One-to-many 
 One source job split by scope or level 
 Split by criteria such as level, team, or country 

 No match 
 No equivalent in the target 
 Create a new job code under governance, or map to the closest with approval 

 Exception 
 Any country specific or regulated roles 
 Keep a separate mapping; involve legal and local HR 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Level mismatch. The same title can mean different scope in each company. Match on scope, accountability, and typical pay, and calibrate with business leaders on a sample of roles. 
 Step 4: Validate and approve 
 Review with HR Center of Excellence, Compensation, Legal, local HR, and business leaders. Start with the jobs covering most of the employees. 
 Run impact analysis for acquired company employees: how many people see a change in title, level, grade, exempt status, or pay position. 
 Engage works councils or employee representatives (unions etc.) where required and build their timeline into the plan. 
 Record every approval in a decision log and set a freeze date after which changes follow change control. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Pay misalignment. Acquired pay can sit outside the target range for the mapped grade. Run the incumbent impact analysis, set an out-of-range policy, and get Compensation approval. 
 Legal and works council constraints. Job grouping and classification can be subject to co-determination or collective agreements. Identify the countries early, involve legal and local HR, and allow consultation time in the plan. 
 Exempt status changes. Classification practices differ between companies. Require counsel sign-off, and model overtime and payroll impact before any change. 
 Late changes after the freeze. Leaders often challenge matches once mock loads begin. Enforce the freeze date, impact assessment, and change control, and quantify the rework. 
 Step 5: Configure in SuccessFactors 
 Create or update job classifications, functions, levels, pay grades and ranges, and picklists with correct effective dates. 
 Set country-specific attributes, and position structures if position management is in use. 
 Align related configuration that depends on job data: role-based permissions, workflows, compensation and performance templates, and recruiting templates. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Missed downstream dependencies. Payroll, recruiting, benefits, workflows, and reports are often keyed to job code, level, or grade. List every dependency during design, configure each one, and test it with real data in Step 6. 
 Step 6: Migrate and test 
 Apply the crosswalk in the data load: each employee’s job information is populated from the mapped target values. 
 Run mock loads with reconciliation by job code, level, grade, and country, and list any incumbent with no match. 
 Test downstream systems that depend on job data: payroll, applicant tracking, benefits eligibility, approval workflows, and reporting. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 History and effective dating. Past job records reference legacy codes. Decide whether history keeps the legacy codes or is remapped, and keep a legacy-to-target reference table for reporting. 
 Step 7: Communicate and govern 
 Brief managers and HR business partners first, with FAQs and talking points. Then communicate to employees. 
 Set up a job-code request process, naming standards, and a periodic review so the architecture does not sprawl after go-live. 
 Retire or lock legacy codes once reporting and history requirements are met. 
 Common issues and how to handle them 
 Perceived demotions or promotions. Title or level changes are visible to employees and managers. Apply the no-decrease and title principles set in Step 2, keep business titles separate from system titles, and br
